Lesson 8 · Guided route

Graphs, comparability and adjustment: guided case

Can an observational comparison recover a program effect?

Follow one business problem from the manager’s request to a practical next step. The business case presents the decision and action plan; the technical appendix holds the complete model and derivations.

Business caseTechnical appendix
Story chapters
  1. 01. A program is offered to different kinds of units
  2. 02. Make like-for-like comparisons
  3. 03. Use the graph to challenge the result

Part 1 of 3

A program is offered to different kinds of units

A manager is asked whether an existing program should be expanded. Program participants do better than nonparticipants by 6.51 units. But participation was not assigned at random: the groups have different starting characteristics. Comparing their final averages would mix program performance with the reasons they entered the program.

The manager first draws a simple causal story. Which characteristics existed before the offer and could affect both selection and outcome? Which measurements were produced after participation began? This ordering is more useful than feeding every available column into a regression.

The program office should map the sequence of events on one page: baseline need, offer, participation, intermediate behavior, and final outcome. That timeline helps a business audience see why adjusting for baseline need may help while adjusting for behavior caused by the program may answer a different question. It also exposes measurements that are missing for one group.

Part 2 of 3

Make like-for-like comparisons

The team groups eligible units by pre-program characteristics where both participants and nonparticipants appear. It calculates a within-group difference, then combines those differences using weights for the population the expansion decision concerns. The resulting standardized average is 2.71 units, much smaller than the raw gap.

How the comparison changes after accounting for starting mix
ComparisonOutcome units
Raw participant gap6.51
Standardized all-unit estimate2.71

Those weights are a business choice as well as a statistical one. A program meant for all eligible units needs a different mix from a program meant only for current participants. Thin comparison cells should be shown to the manager rather than hidden inside one reassuring adjusted number.

Within each stratum, the analyst asks what happened to participants and comparable nonparticipants. The combined answer depends on which strata receive more weight. A network-wide expansion gives weight to all eligible units; a service improvement for current participants gives more weight to their mix. Making that choice visible prevents a technically correct estimate from answering the wrong budget question.

Part 3 of 3

Use the graph to challenge the result

The causal diagram explains why a good predictor is not always a good control. If a variable is a consequence of participation, adjusting for it can remove part of the program’s effect. If it is a common consequence of two earlier causes, adjustment can create a false association. The point of the diagram is to make these choices discussable before the result is known.

For the expansion memo, report the adjusted comparison, the target population, and the strata with weak overlap. Then identify one plausible unmeasured reason for selection that would most change the recommendation. That is a more useful next investigation than adding controls simply to improve fit.

The next action is to review the thin cells and the business reasons for program selection. If some eligible units have no credible comparison, the manager could pilot the program there rather than extrapolate an adjusted average. The analysis is most valuable when it clarifies where a decision is supported and where the organization should collect stronger evidence.

Decision check

Why not include every variable that predicts the outcome?

Compare your reasoning

Some variables occur after the program or are common consequences of other causes. Their timing and causal role determine whether adjustment helps.

Check your judgment

Reveal the case’s known answer

The case’s average program effect is 2.70 units. Compare it with the standardized estimate to see how much the starting mix changed the raw gap.

The bigger picture

When a program already exists, the organization may have to learn from how it was assigned in ordinary operations. The crucial work is to reconstruct the selection process, compare units with similar starting conditions, and give weight to the people the decision will affect. That connects the estimate to an expansion plan. It also shows where a new pilot would be valuable. The next lesson turns this reasoning into a facility-level evaluation and asks how to report a result for the exact population covered by a budget.
